moments.title: De revolutionibus published
moments.body:
Copernicus's heliocentric model is published in the year of his death.

Its mathematics is comparable in complexity to Ptolemy's, but it places the Sun at the centre.
moments.takeaway: A simpler conceptual model was, in calculation, no simpler than its rival.

moments.title: Galileo's telescope observations
moments.body:
Galileo's improved telescope reveals lunar craters, Jupiter's moons, Venus's phases and sunspots.

The phases of Venus are direct evidence against Ptolemy's system.
moments.takeaway: An instrument decided a centuries-long debate.

moments.title: Newton's Principia
moments.body: Newton derives planetary motion from universal gravitation. The Royal Society publishes the Principia at Edmond Halley's expense.
moments.takeaway: Empirical celestial mechanics and a single mathematical framework unified.

now.title: Cosmology today
now.body: General relativity, expansion of space and standard cosmological model frame current research. Open problems include dark matter, dark energy and the Hubble tension.
now.open_questions: What is dark energy? Why do different methods give different values for the Hubble constant?

items.reflection: Heliocentrism is now intuitive in education; in 1600 it was an institutional fight that destroyed careers.

moments.title: Lemaitre derives the expansion
moments.body: Lemaitre publishes the relationship between redshift and distance in French two years before Hubble's English paper.
moments.takeaway: Language and venue affected credit for what is now the Hubble-Lemaitre Law.

moments.title: Hubble's paper
moments.body: Hubble's English-language paper presents distance-redshift data for nearby galaxies, supporting cosmic expansion.
moments.takeaway: Observation and theory met in different journals and languages.

moments.title: Cosmic microwave background discovered
moments.body: Penzias and Wilson detect a uniform microwave signal initially treated as noise. Dicke's Princeton group identifies it as the relic radiation predicted by Big Bang cosmology.
moments.takeaway: Major theoretical predictions can be verified accidentally.

now.title: Modern cosmology
now.body: Precision measurements from WMAP, Planck and surveys like DES refine cosmological parameters. JWST and the Vera Rubin Observatory will extend the data baseline.
now.open_questions: Why is matter so unevenly distributed? Will the Hubble tension be resolved by new physics or systematics?

items.reflection: Cosmology has shifted from a speculative branch of astronomy to a precision science within a single human lifetime.

moments.title: Hubble Space Telescope launched
moments.who: NASA and ESA, Space Shuttle Discovery
moments.body:
Hubble launches with a flawed primary mirror. The 1993 servicing mission corrects the optics.

Hubble produces transformative deep-field images and exoplanet atmosphere data.
moments.takeaway: Space-based observatories combine extraordinary capability with risky logistics.

moments.title: First exoplanet around a sunlike star
moments.who: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, Geneva
moments.body: 51 Pegasi b is detected by radial velocity. Mayor and Queloz share the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.
moments.takeaway: Astronomy's exoplanet era began with a single detection.

moments.title: JWST launch and first images
moments.body: JWST launches on 25 December 2021 and releases its first science images on 12 July 2022.
moments.takeaway: A 30-year project produced data that immediately reshaped early-universe astronomy.

now.title: Observatories today
now.body: JWST, Vera Rubin Observatory and ESO's Extremely Large Telescope (under construction) push deeper across wavelengths. Space-based gravitational wave detectors are planned.
now.open_questions: How early can JWST trace galaxy formation? What can we learn about exoplanet atmospheres?

items.reflection: Major instruments depend on decadal planning and international collaboration in scientific bodies that are increasingly under political strain.

moments.title: Zwicky on cluster mass
moments.body: Zwicky's analysis of the Coma cluster requires far more mass than visible to explain the velocities of galaxies, coining 'dunkle Materie'.
moments.takeaway: Early evidence for dark matter was overlooked for decades.

moments.title: Rubin's flat rotation curves
moments.body: Rotation curves of spiral galaxies stay flat at large radii, implying substantial unseen mass.
moments.takeaway: Direct kinematic measurements made dark matter unavoidable.

moments.title: Accelerating expansion
moments.body: Type Ia supernova observations indicate the expansion of the universe is accelerating, inviting the term 'dark energy'.
moments.takeaway: Two of three independent observations changed the cosmic budget.

now.title: Dark sector today
now.body: About 27% of the universe is modelled as dark matter and 68% as dark energy. Direct detection experiments (e.g. LZ, XENONnT) and surveys (DESI, Euclid) seek further constraints.
now.open_questions: Are dark matter and dark energy single phenomena? Could modifications of gravity replace them?

items.reflection: Most of the universe's energy budget is described by negative results: things we have not detected directly.

moments.title: Stonehenge built and rebuilt
moments.who: Neolithic and early Bronze Age Britons
moments.body: Stonehenge's main sarsen circle is erected around 2500 BCE. The Heel Stone aligns with sunrise on the summer solstice; the central trilithon frames sunset on the winter solstice. Earlier wooden post arrangements at Stonehenge and at Durrington Walls show solar alignment was a long-standing concern.
moments.takeaway: Pre-literate societies built precise solar observatories. Astronomy predates writing by millennia.

moments.title: The Nebra Sky Disc
moments.body: Discovered in 1999 in Germany, the Nebra Sky Disc (c.1600 BCE) shows the Sun, crescent Moon, the Pleiades cluster and what may be a depiction of a solar boat. The angle between the solstices at the disc's latitude is precisely marked.
moments.takeaway: The earliest known concrete representation of the sky is European Bronze Age — and contains astronomical measurement.

now.title: Archaeoastronomy today
now.body: Sites from Newgrange (Ireland, c.3200 BCE) to Chankillo (Peru, c.300 BCE) to Mayan Chichen Itza show solar/lunar alignments built into architecture. English Heritage now hosts ~10,000 visitors at Stonehenge for the summer solstice.
now.open_questions: Were alignments primarily religious, agricultural-calendrical, or both? Most likely both, but the boundary is modern.

items.reflection: The questions that drove astronomy — when to plant, when to feast, what governs the year — predate the questions that drove writing. Knowing the sky was a survival skill.

moments.title: Babylonian astronomers
moments.body: Babylonian astronomers compile centuries of planetary observations on cuneiform tablets, predict eclipses using the Saros cycle (~18 years), and develop arithmetic methods for predicting planetary positions. The 'MUL.APIN' tablets (c.1000 BCE) catalogue 71 stars.
moments.takeaway: Quantitative observational astronomy in Mesopotamia predates Greek astronomy by centuries. The Greeks inherited the data.

moments.title: Hipparchus and stellar precession
moments.body: Hipparchus catalogues 850 stars with positions, develops a magnitude scale (still used in modified form), and — by comparing with earlier Babylonian and Greek observations — discovers the precession of the equinoxes (~1° per century; actual: 1° every 72 years). He invents trigonometry to support the work.
moments.takeaway: An ancient Greek astronomer discovered the slow wobble of Earth's axis by comparing his star positions to records 150 years older.

moments.title: Ptolemy's Almagest
moments.body: Ptolemy's Mathematical Syntaxis (later known by its Arabic name al-majisti, 'the Almagest') systematises Greek astronomy with a geocentric model: Earth at centre, planets on epicycles riding deferents, with the equant as an extra geometric trick to fit observations. The model predicts planetary positions to ~1° for over 1,400 years.
moments.takeaway: The 'wrong' geocentric model worked well enough to dominate astronomy for fourteen centuries. Predictive accuracy and physical reality are not the same.

now.title: Ancient astronomy today
now.body: Babylonian eclipse records remain useful for measuring Earth's slowing rotation (changes in length of day). Hipparchus' star catalogue is largely lost; ESA's Hipparcos mission (1989-93) was named for him. Greek and Arabic astronomical manuscripts were preserved through Islamic Golden Age scholarship (Al-Battani, Al-Sufi, Ibn al-Haytham).
now.open_questions: How much earlier astronomy did Babylonian observers inherit from even older Sumerian sources? Tablets are still being found and translated.

items.reflection: Western astronomy until 1543 ran on Greek geometry, Babylonian data and Arabic improvements. The story of who 'did' astronomy depends on what counts as astronomy.

moments.title: Tycho's supernova
moments.body: On 11 November 1572, Brahe observes a 'new star' (now known to be a Type Ia supernova) in Cassiopeia, brighter than Venus, visible for 16 months. The unchanging celestial sphere is supposed to be unchanging. Brahe's 'De Nova Stella' (1573) — from which we get 'nova' — shakes Aristotelian cosmology.
moments.takeaway: A single supernova ended the philosophical principle that the heavens were immutable. The data won.

moments.title: Kepler's first two laws
moments.body: Inheriting Brahe's precise observations of Mars after Brahe's death (1601), Kepler spends years fitting circles to the data — failing by 8 arcminutes. He tries ellipses. They fit. Astronomia Nova (1609) publishes the first (elliptical orbits) and second (equal areas in equal times) laws. The third law (T² ∝ a³) follows in 1619.

quote.text: Eight minutes of arc... showed the way to the reformation of the whole of astronomy.

moments.takeaway: Kepler's commitment to data over preconception — Mars's orbit had to be elliptical, not circular — broke 2,000 years of celestial circles.

now.title: Orbital mechanics today
now.body: Kepler's laws describe every orbit in the solar system, every artificial satellite, every exoplanet system. The Kepler space telescope (2009-2018) is named for him. Modern mission design adds perturbation theory, n-body simulations and relativistic corrections, but Kepler's laws remain the starting point.
now.open_questions: How much credit belongs to Brahe? Without his observations, Kepler had nothing. Without Kepler's analysis, the observations remained data.

items.reflection: Brahe lost most of his nose in a duel over a mathematics dispute and wore a brass prosthesis. Kepler was court astrologer and defended his mother in her witchcraft trial. Science was practised by humans in the world they inhabited.

moments.title: Halley predicts the return
moments.body: Applying Newton's gravity to comet observations, Halley argues that the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 are the same body, and predicts its return in 1758. Halley dies in 1742. The comet returns, on Christmas Day 1758, as predicted.
moments.takeaway: The first major successful prediction of a celestial event by Newtonian gravity made physics a public spectacle.

now.title: Comets today
now.body: Halley's Comet returns roughly every 76 years; last seen 1986, next return 2061. Rosetta (2014) orbited and landed Philae on comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, sampling cometary material. Interstellar visitors (1I/'Oumuamua 2017, 2I/Borisov 2019) extend the catalogue.
now.open_questions: Where do long-period comets come from? The Oort cloud is hypothesised but not directly observed.

items.reflection: Halley funded and edited the publication of Newton's Principia from his own pocket. Without him there is no Principia; without Principia there is no Halley's Comet. Scientific reputation is often a function of who supports whom.

moments.title: Cavendish weighs the Earth
moments.body: Cavendish uses a torsion balance designed by John Michell (deceased) to measure the gravitational attraction between lead balls in his laboratory. From this he derives Earth's density (5.448 times water; modern value 5.515). The experiment is precise to ~1% — extraordinary for 1798.
moments.takeaway: The first laboratory measurement of gravity yielded a value for G — and so for Earth's mass — accurate to a fraction of a percent.

now.title: Measuring G today
now.body: G is still one of the worst-measured fundamental constants: CODATA value 6.67430×10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg² with relative uncertainty ~2.2×10⁻⁵. Different experimental methods give discrepant values. The pace of improvement is slow.
now.open_questions: Why is G so much harder to measure than other constants? Possible answers include the weakness of gravity at lab scales and systematic effects unique to torsion balances.

items.reflection: Cavendish was so socially anxious he reportedly communicated with female servants only by written note. He published a fraction of his work. Maxwell, editing his unpublished papers in 1879, found Cavendish had anticipated Ohm's Law, Coulomb's Law and Faraday's work decades earlier.

moments.title: Bessel measures stellar parallax
moments.body: Bessel announces the parallax of 61 Cygni: 0.314 arcseconds (modern value: 0.286 arcseconds), giving a distance of ~10.3 light years. He has measured the apparent shift of the star against background stars as Earth moves around the Sun, finally settling a debate that goes back to Aristotle.
moments.takeaway: The first successful measurement of stellar distance ended 2,000 years of speculation. Stars were real bodies at real, measurable distances.

now.title: Parallax today
now.body: ESA's Gaia mission (2013-present) is measuring parallaxes for ~1.8 billion stars with microarcsecond precision — extending the reliable parallax method to ~10,000 light years. Beyond that, the cosmic distance ladder (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) builds outward.
now.open_questions: The Gaia parallax data are causing tension in the Hubble constant measurement. Are systematic errors in distance scales contributing?

items.reflection: Bessel's measurement was so precise it required eliminating effects (refraction, aberration, the motion of 61 Cygni itself) that astronomy had only recently discovered. Each new precision generates new categories of error to manage.

moments.title: Cannon classifies 350,000 stars
moments.who: Annie Jump Cannon, Harvard College Observatory
moments.body: Cannon, working among the 'Harvard Computers' (a team of women paid 25 cents an hour to analyse stellar spectra under Edward Pickering), refines the spectral classification system to OBAFGKM — by temperature, not by hydrogen-line strength as earlier classifications had assumed. She personally classifies over 350,000 stars. The Henry Draper Catalogue (1918-24) becomes the standard.
moments.takeaway: The classification system used in every modern astronomy textbook was built by one woman over a quarter-century, surrounded by colleagues paid less than typists.

moments.title: Leavitt's period-luminosity law
moments.who: Henrietta Swan Leavitt, Harvard College Observatory
moments.body: Leavitt, another Harvard Computer, discovers that Cepheid variable stars have a period-luminosity relationship: brighter Cepheids pulse more slowly. This means a Cepheid's brightness can be calibrated from its period, making them 'standard candles' for measuring distance.
moments.takeaway: Leavitt's law later allowed Hubble to measure that Andromeda was outside the Milky Way and the universe was expanding. She died of cancer in 1921 at 53, before her work transformed cosmology.

now.title: Spectroscopy today
now.body: OBAFGKM classification is universal; the mnemonic 'Oh Be A Fine Girl/Guy Kiss Me' has its own awkward history. Spectral classification has been extended (L, T, Y for brown dwarfs). Cepheid standard candles remain a key rung of the distance ladder. The Annie Jump Cannon Award and the Henrietta Swan Leavitt Award honour their namesakes.
now.open_questions: How are the spectra of the very earliest stars (Population III) different? JWST is starting to answer.

items.reflection: The Harvard Computers — Cannon, Leavitt, Williamina Fleming, Antonia Maury — produced a generation of foundational astronomy. They were called 'Pickering's Harem' at the time. Dava Sobel's 'The Glass Universe' (2016) restored their story.

moments.title: Hertzsprung-Russell diagram
moments.who: Ejnar Hertzsprung (Denmark) and Henry Norris Russell (Princeton)
moments.body: Independently, Hertzsprung (1911) and Russell (1913) plot stellar luminosity against temperature (or spectral type). Most stars lie along a diagonal 'main sequence'; giants and dwarfs lie elsewhere. The diagram becomes the foundation of stellar evolution theory.
moments.takeaway: A single plot organised all stellar astrophysics. The H-R diagram remains the most-used summary tool in stellar astronomy.

now.title: Stellar evolution today
now.body: We now understand the H-R diagram as a snapshot of stars at different masses and evolutionary stages. Main sequence: hydrogen fusion in the core. Giants: hydrogen-shell burning, expanded envelope. White dwarfs: stellar remnants. JWST is sharpening early-universe stellar populations.
now.open_questions: How does stellar evolution differ at very low metallicity (early universe stars)? Population III stars have not been directly observed.

items.reflection: Hertzsprung was an engineer; Russell was a theorist. The diagram named for both of them was produced independently in different countries with different methods. Sometimes science converges.

moments.title: Cecilia Payne's PhD thesis
moments.body: Payne's PhD thesis 'Stellar Atmospheres' applies Meghnad Saha's ionisation theory to stellar spectra and concludes that stars are overwhelmingly composed of hydrogen and helium — not, as accepted wisdom held, of the same elemental mix as Earth. Henry Norris Russell pressures her to call the result 'spurious'. He retracts four years later, after independent confirmation.

quote.text: The most brilliant PhD thesis ever written in astronomy.

moments.takeaway: A 24-year-old woman discovered what stars are made of. She was forced to disavow her own correct result and watched a male astronomer claim credit.

now.title: Stellar composition today
now.body: Hydrogen ~74% by mass, helium ~24%, everything else <2% — Payne was right. Stellar nucleosynthesis (Burbidge, Burbidge, Fowler, Hoyle 1957, 'B²FH') traces heavier elements to stars. We are made of star-stuff. Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin became Harvard's first female full professor in 1956 — 31 years after her thesis.
now.open_questions: How metal-poor were the first stars? JWST observations of high-redshift galaxies are pushing the boundary.

items.reflection: Russell's 1929 paper confirming Payne's hydrogen-dominance result is one of the most-cited papers in astronomy. Payne is mentioned in a footnote.

moments.title: Chandrasekhar's calculation
moments.who: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, on a voyage from India to Cambridge
moments.body: Aged 19, on a ship to begin doctoral studies in Cambridge, Chandrasekhar calculates that white dwarfs cannot exist above ~1.4 solar masses; electron degeneracy pressure cannot resist gravity. The implication: more massive stellar cores must collapse further — into neutron stars or black holes. Arthur Eddington publicly mocks the result in 1935.
moments.takeaway: A 19-year-old on a boat predicted black holes. The establishment took 30 years to accept it.

now.title: Stellar remnants today
now.body: The Chandrasekhar limit (~1.44 solar masses) explains Type Ia supernovae: a white dwarf accretes mass, hits the limit, undergoes thermonuclear runaway. The standardised brightness of these explosions makes them 'standard candles' that revealed accelerating expansion (1998). Chandrasekhar received the 1983 Nobel Prize.
now.open_questions: Are there sub-Chandrasekhar Type Ia mechanisms? The picture has been complicated by recent observations.

items.reflection: Chandrasekhar moved from India to Cambridge to Yerkes Observatory in Wisconsin, where he commuted hundreds of miles to teach a graduate class of two students. They both won Nobel Prizes (Lee, Yang, 1957). The teacher won his in 1983.

moments.title: Herschel maps the Milky Way
moments.body: Herschel's 'On the Construction of the Heavens' uses star counts to argue the Milky Way is a disc-shaped system. Caroline Herschel, his sister and collaborator, discovers eight comets and catalogues nebulae. William also discovers Uranus (1781), infrared radiation (1800) and over 2,500 nebulae.
moments.takeaway: The first attempt to map our galaxy's shape was made by a brother-sister team in 18th-century England. Caroline was the first woman paid as an astronomer.

moments.title: The Great Debate: Curtis vs Shapley
moments.who: Heber Curtis (Lick) and Harlow Shapley (Mount Wilson)
moments.body: At the Smithsonian on 26 April 1920, Curtis and Shapley debate whether spiral nebulae are inside the Milky Way (Shapley) or separate galaxies (Curtis). Each is half-right: Shapley correctly enlarges the Milky Way; Curtis correctly identifies spiral nebulae as external galaxies. The debate is settled by Hubble in 1924.
moments.takeaway: The size of the universe was openly debated by professional astronomers within living memory. We did not know we were in a galaxy among galaxies a century ago.

moments.title: Hubble resolves Andromeda
moments.body: Using the 100-inch Hooker telescope on Mount Wilson and Leavitt's Cepheid period-luminosity relation, Hubble measures the distance to the Andromeda 'nebula' (M31): ~900,000 light years (modern: 2.5 million). It is far outside the Milky Way. The universe contains other galaxies.
moments.takeaway: On a single photographic plate Hubble's note 'VAR!' next to a Cepheid in Andromeda effectively settled the question. The plate is preserved at Carnegie Observatories.

now.title: Galaxies today
now.body: Observable universe: ~2 trillion galaxies (JWST has revised this estimate upward). The Milky Way is one spiral galaxy in the Local Group, which is part of the Virgo Supercluster, which is part of Laniakea. We are still mapping the local structure.
now.open_questions: How did the first galaxies form? JWST is observing galaxies at z>10 (less than 500 million years after the Big Bang) that are larger and more mature than models predicted.

items.reflection: Caroline Herschel received a salary of £50/year from George III in 1787 — the first woman paid as a professional astronomer. She lived to 97 (died 1848) and received the Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society in 1828.

moments.title: Alpher, Bethe and Gamow predict the CMB
moments.who: Ralph Alpher, Hans Bethe, George Gamow
moments.body: Their 'αβγ' paper (Gamow added Bethe's name for the alphabetical pun) calculates primordial nucleosynthesis in a hot early universe. A companion paper (Alpher and Herman, 1948) predicts a relic background radiation at ~5 K. The prediction is essentially ignored for 17 years.
moments.takeaway: The cosmic microwave background was predicted in 1948 and discovered accidentally in 1965 by people unaware of the prediction.

moments.title: Hoyle vs Big Bang
moments.who: Fred Hoyle (Cambridge), Hermann Bondi, Thomas Gold
moments.body: Hoyle coins 'Big Bang' on a 1949 BBC radio programme — derisively. He advocates the Steady State model (continuous matter creation). The 1965 CMB discovery decisively favours Big Bang. Hoyle never fully accepts it. He continues important work on stellar nucleosynthesis.
moments.takeaway: The dominant name for the dominant cosmological model was coined by its leading opponent as a mockery.

moments.title: COBE maps CMB anisotropy
moments.who: John Mather and George Smoot, COBE team
moments.body: The Cosmic Background Explorer's first results show the CMB is a near-perfect blackbody at 2.725 K with anisotropies at the 10⁻⁵ level — the seeds of all later structure. Stephen Hawking calls it 'the greatest discovery of the century, if not of all time'. Mather and Smoot share the 2006 Nobel Prize.
moments.takeaway: Tiny temperature variations in the CMB are the imprints of quantum fluctuations from the universe's first 10⁻³² seconds.

now.title: CMB today
now.body: Planck satellite (2009-13) measurements give the most precise cosmological parameters: age 13.787 ± 0.020 Gyr, H₀ ≈ 67.4 km/s/Mpc (in tension with local measurements giving ~73). Future missions (LiteBIRD, CMB-S4) will look for primordial gravitational waves in CMB polarisation.
now.open_questions: Is the Hubble tension a sign of new physics or systematic errors? Was there cosmic inflation, and if so what drove it?

items.reflection: Gamow was Russian-born, worked in Germany and Denmark before defecting to the US in 1933. The Big Bang model was developed by Belgian Catholic priest (Lemaître), Russian émigré (Gamow), and American radio astronomers — a 20th-century international science narrative.

moments.title: Jocelyn Bell discovers pulsars
moments.body: Bell, a PhD student under Antony Hewish, notices regular pulses (1.337-second period) in radio data from the Mullard Radio Astronomy Observatory. She and Hewish initially label the source 'LGM-1' (Little Green Men). Further sources rule out artificial origin; they are rapidly rotating neutron stars with intense magnetic fields. The 1974 Nobel Prize goes to Hewish (and Martin Ryle), not Bell.
moments.takeaway: Bell's careful, slow attention to a tiny anomaly in her thesis data revealed an entirely new class of cosmic object.

now.title: Pulsars today
now.body: Over 3,000 pulsars are catalogued. Millisecond pulsars rival atomic clocks in stability. Pulsar timing arrays (NANOGrav, EPTA, PPTA) detected the gravitational wave background from supermassive black hole mergers in 2023. The Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar (1974) provided indirect evidence of gravitational waves (Nobel 1993).
now.open_questions: What is the equation of state of nuclear matter inside a neutron star? NICER on the ISS is making precise measurements.

items.reflection: Bell Burnell was awarded the $3 million Breakthrough Prize in 2018, decades after the Nobel snub. She donated it to fund PhD studentships for women, ethnic-minority and refugee students entering physics.

moments.title: Voyager 1 and 2 launch
moments.body: Voyager 2 launches on 20 August 1977; Voyager 1 on 5 September 1977. A rare planetary alignment (occurs once every 175 years) permits a gravity-assist 'Grand Tour' of the outer planets. Voyager 1 flies past Jupiter (1979), Saturn (1980). Voyager 2 also visits Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989) — still the only spacecraft to do so.
moments.takeaway: Two spacecraft, designed for 5-year missions, are now in interstellar space (Voyager 1 in 2012, Voyager 2 in 2018) and still returning data nearly 50 years later.

moments.title: Pale Blue Dot
moments.body: On 14 February 1990, at Sagan's urging, Voyager 1 turns its camera back at the solar system from 6 billion km away. Earth appears as a sub-pixel dot — the 'Pale Blue Dot'. Sagan's 1994 reflection becomes one of the most-quoted passages in popular science.

quote.text: On it everyone you love, everyone you know, everyone you ever heard of, every human being who ever was, lived out their lives.

moments.takeaway: The view of Earth from 6 billion km redefined every framing of human conflict.

now.title: Outer planet exploration today
now.body: Galileo (Jupiter 1995-2003), Cassini-Huygens (Saturn 1997-2017), New Horizons (Pluto 2015), Juno (Jupiter 2016-), Europa Clipper (launched 2024), JUICE (launched 2023). Cassini's controlled plunge into Saturn (15 September 2017) ended an extraordinary mission.
now.open_questions: What is under Europa's ice? Could Enceladus's plumes carry life out for sampling? Missions are being designed.

items.reflection: Each Voyager carries a Golden Record: greetings in 55 languages, music from Bach to Chuck Berry, sounds of Earth. The records will outlast the Sun. We sent a love letter to the universe without knowing if anyone could read it.

moments.title: Kennedy commits to the Moon
moments.who: President John F. Kennedy, US Congress
moments.body: On 25 May 1961, Kennedy commits the US to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely 'before this decade is out'. The Soviets had just launched Gagarin (12 April 1961). Apollo budget peaks at 4.4% of US federal spending in 1966.
moments.takeaway: A political commitment in May 1961 produced a Moon landing in July 1969 — eight years from commitment to footprint.

moments.title: Apollo 11 lands
moments.who: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, Michael Collins
moments.body: On 20 July 1969 at 20:17 UTC, Armstrong and Aldrin land on Mare Tranquillitatis. Armstrong steps onto the surface at 02:56 UTC on 21 July. 600 million people — a fifth of humanity — watch live. Margaret Hamilton's onboard guidance software handles a 1202 alarm during landing without crashing.

quote.text: That's one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind.

moments.takeaway: The Apollo Guidance Computer ran on 4KB of RAM and 72KB of ROM. Modern AAA batteries are programmed with more code than landed humans on the Moon.

now.title: Lunar exploration today
now.body: After Apollo 17 (1972), no humans returned to the Moon for 50+ years. China's Chang'e program has landed rovers (2013-) and returned samples (2020, 2024 including first far-side return). NASA's Artemis program targets human return in the late 2020s. SpaceX, Blue Origin and private actors are now major spaceflight players.
now.open_questions: Will humans build permanent lunar habitats this century? Water ice at the lunar south pole is the strategic resource.

items.reflection: Of the 12 men who walked on the Moon (all American men), 4 remain alive in 2026. The longest-living Apollo astronaut, Buzz Aldrin, turned 96 this year. Living memory of human presence on another world is ending.

moments.title: Viking lands on Mars
moments.body: Viking 1 lands in Chryse Planitia on 20 July 1976 (seven years to the day after Apollo 11). It returns the first colour photographs from Mars's surface and conducts biology experiments. The experimental results remain ambiguous — Gilbert Levin (Viking biology PI) maintained until his death (2021) that they were positive for microbial life.
moments.takeaway: The first soft landing on Mars conducted biology experiments before the equipment to interpret them properly existed.

moments.title: Sojourner rover
moments.body: The 11kg Sojourner rover (Mars Pathfinder mission) is the first wheeled vehicle on another planet. It operates for 83 days against a planned 7. Subsequent rovers — Spirit and Opportunity (2004), Curiosity (2012), Perseverance (2021) — became progressively larger and more autonomous. Opportunity worked for 14 years.
moments.takeaway: Mars rovers have continuously operated on Mars almost without break since 2004. Mars exploration is older than most current undergraduates.

now.title: Mars today
now.body: Perseverance is caching samples for a planned Mars Sample Return mission (delayed and rescoped, mid-2030s). Ingenuity, its helicopter companion, conducted 72 flights — the first powered flight on another planet (April 2021). SpaceX targets uncrewed Starship missions in the late 2020s.
now.open_questions: Did life ever exist on Mars? The samples being cached may answer this — if returned.

items.reflection: Two-thirds of Mars missions in history have failed. Mars Climate Orbiter (1999) was lost because one team used metric units and another used imperial. Even at planetary scale, units matter.

moments.title: Drake equation
moments.body: At a small Green Bank, West Virginia meeting (10 attendees including Carl Sagan), Drake writes down an equation estimating the number of communicating civilisations in our galaxy: N = R* × fp × ne × fl × fi × fc × L. Each term has wildly uncertain ranges. The equation organises the search rather than predicting an answer.
moments.takeaway: The Drake equation reframed alien life from a metaphysical question to an empirical (if very uncertain) one.

moments.title: Wow! signal
moments.who: Jerry Ehman, Ohio State Big Ear telescope
moments.body: On 15 August 1977, a 72-second narrowband signal at 1420 MHz (hydrogen line) is recorded. Ehman writes 'Wow!' on the printout. The signal has never been re-detected despite many attempts. Origin remains unknown.
moments.takeaway: The most provocative SETI signal in history was either a one-off natural event, an artificial signal we'll never confirm, or instrument noise.

now.title: SETI today
now.body: Breakthrough Listen (2015-) is the largest SETI program ever, scanning the nearest million stars and 100 nearest galaxies. JWST analyses exoplanet atmospheres for biosignatures (oxygen, methane, dimethyl sulfide). Mars sample return and Europa Clipper extend in-system search. No confirmed signal in 60+ years of searching.
now.open_questions: Where is everybody? (Fermi's question, 1950). If life is common, why no evidence? Hypotheses: rare Earth, great filter, dark forest, simulation.

items.reflection: Fermi posed his question over lunch at Los Alamos in 1950. Seventy-five years of search has produced no positive answers. The silence is itself data.

moments.title: 51 Pegasi b
moments.who: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, Geneva
moments.body: On 6 October 1995 at a conference in Florence, Mayor and Queloz announce a Jupiter-mass planet orbiting a Sun-like star at 0.05 AU with a 4.2-day period. The discovery overturns assumptions about where giant planets can form. Mayor and Queloz share the 2019 Nobel Prize.
moments.takeaway: The first exoplanet around a sunlike star was a 'hot Jupiter' — a category nobody had predicted. The universe's planetary systems were stranger than the solar system suggested.

moments.title: Kepler mission
moments.body: The Kepler space telescope monitors ~150,000 stars for transits, discovering ~2,700 confirmed exoplanets. Statistical analysis suggests every star in the Milky Way has on average at least one planet. Earth-sized planets in habitable zones are common.
moments.takeaway: Planets are not rare. They are everywhere. The question shifted from 'are there other planets?' to 'are there other Earths?'

moments.title: TRAPPIST-1 system
moments.body: Seven Earth-sized planets are found around the ultracool dwarf TRAPPIST-1, 40 light years away. Three are in the habitable zone. JWST is now characterising their atmospheres.
moments.takeaway: A single nearby system contains seven small rocky worlds. Tightly packed systems are common.

now.title: Exoplanets today
now.body: Over 5,500 confirmed exoplanets (NASA Exoplanet Archive, 2024). TESS continues the survey. JWST is producing exoplanet atmosphere spectra. The Habitable Worlds Observatory (NASA, planned 2040s) is being designed to image Earth-like worlds directly.
now.open_questions: Is there a biosphere on a nearby exoplanet? Atmospheric biosignatures (O₂ + CH₄ in disequilibrium, DMS) are the current targets.

items.reflection: When Mayor was a student, no exoplanets were known. He has lived through their entire scientific history — from non-existent to a confirmed catalogue of thousands. Few astronomers see a field begin and mature in their career.

moments.title: Einstein predicts gravitational waves
moments.body: Einstein's general relativity (1915) predicts gravitational waves — ripples in spacetime travelling at the speed of light. The amplitudes are so tiny he doubts they can ever be detected. He briefly retracts the prediction in 1936; reviewer Howard Robertson convinces him it was right.
moments.takeaway: A prediction at the limit of theoretical credibility took 100 years and unprecedented instrumental precision to confirm.

moments.title: GW150914
moments.body: On 14 September 2015 at 09:50:45 UTC, both LIGO detectors (Hanford WA and Livingston LA) record a gravitational wave signal: two black holes (~36 and ~29 solar masses) merging 1.3 billion light years away. The peak strain was ~10⁻²¹ — measuring a 4km arm length change of 1/10,000 the width of a proton. Announcement: 11 February 2016. 2017 Nobel Prize.
moments.takeaway: Humans built an instrument sensitive enough to hear two black holes colliding in another galaxy a billion years ago.

now.title: Gravitational wave astronomy today
now.body: LIGO, Virgo and KAGRA have detected ~100 mergers. GW170817 (neutron star merger, 2017) was observed across the electromagnetic spectrum — multi-messenger astronomy was born. NANOGrav (2023) detected the supermassive black hole merger background using pulsar timing. LISA (planned 2035) will be a space-based detector.
now.open_questions: Are there primordial gravitational waves from cosmic inflation? CMB polarisation experiments are searching.

items.reflection: LIGO is a billion-dollar instrument that was approved largely on faith in Kip Thorne, Rainer Weiss and Ronald Drever. They proposed it in the 1980s, started construction in the 1990s, ran for years without seeing anything, and detected GW150914 four days after Advanced LIGO's design sensitivity came online.

moments.title: Schwarzschild solution
moments.body: Months after Einstein publishes general relativity, German astronomer Karl Schwarzschild — serving in the German artillery on the Eastern Front — produces the first exact solution to Einstein's field equations. The solution implies an event horizon at r = 2GM/c². Schwarzschild dies of a skin disease (pemphigus) months later, before seeing his work published.
moments.takeaway: The mathematics of black holes was worked out in the trenches of WWI by a man who would not live to see his work in print.

moments.title: First image of a black hole (M87*)
moments.body: On 10 April 2019, the EHT releases the first image of a black hole: the supermassive black hole at the centre of M87, mass ~6.5 billion suns, 55 million light years away. The image combines data from 8 radio telescopes across the globe — a virtual telescope the size of Earth. Katie Bouman's image-reconstruction algorithm becomes famous.
moments.takeaway: An image we were told was impossible was made by combining data from telescopes on four continents.

moments.title: Sgr A* imaged
moments.body: On 12 May 2022, the EHT releases the image of Sgr A*, the 4-million-solar-mass black hole at the centre of the Milky Way. Imaging Sgr A* is harder than M87 because it varies on shorter timescales.
moments.takeaway: We have directly imaged the black hole at the centre of our own galaxy.

now.title: Black holes today
now.body: EHT is expanding (next-generation EHT). Hawking radiation (1974) remains theoretically predicted but undetected. The information paradox (does information escape black holes?) remains contested. JWST has found supermassive black holes at high redshift larger than formation models predict.
now.open_questions: How did supermassive black holes grow so large so fast in the early universe? Direct-collapse origin or rapid accretion?

items.reflection: Karl Schwarzschild's son Martin became a leading 20th-century astrophysicist at Princeton. Black holes — Schwarzschild's mathematics — were imaged by another generation entirely. Discoveries outlive their discoverers in ways that lesser work does not.

moments.title: Hawking radiation
moments.body: Hawking's paper 'Particle Creation by Black Holes' (Nature, 1974) shows that quantum effects near the event horizon cause black holes to radiate as if they had a temperature T = ℏc³/(8πGMk_B). Small black holes evaporate; the predicted Hawking temperature for a stellar-mass black hole is ~10⁻⁷ K — far too cold to observe against the CMB.
moments.takeaway: A theoretical insight at the boundary of quantum mechanics and gravity remains untested 50 years later because the predicted signal is too cold to detect.

now.title: Quantum gravity today
now.body: Hawking radiation has been observed in analogue systems (sonic event horizons in BEC, etc.), but not from actual black holes. The black hole information paradox — does Hawking radiation carry away information? — remains contested. AdS/CFT correspondence (Maldacena 1997) suggests information is preserved. Hawking conceded the bet to Preskill in 2004.
now.open_questions: Is gravity quantised? String theory and loop quantum gravity offer different answers; experiments cannot yet distinguish.

items.reflection: Hawking was diagnosed with ALS at 21 and given two years to live; he lived to 76. He bet against the existence of black holes (he conceded to Kip Thorne, 1990) and against information preservation. Some of his most-cited work argues for ideas he later abandoned.

moments.title: Guth proposes inflation
moments.body: Guth proposes that the very early universe (~10⁻³⁶ to 10⁻³² seconds after the Big Bang) underwent exponential expansion driven by a false-vacuum scalar field. Inflation solves the horizon problem (why the CMB is uniform across causally disconnected regions), the flatness problem (why Ω is so close to 1), and predicts quantum fluctuations as seeds of structure.
moments.takeaway: A 10⁻³⁴ second epoch reshapes the entire observable universe. Cosmological models propagate from instants we cannot directly observe.

now.title: Inflation today
now.body: Inflation is the standard early-universe model but lacks direct evidence. CMB polarisation B-modes from primordial gravitational waves would be a smoking gun — BICEP2 (2014) claimed detection but it turned out to be galactic dust. CMB-S4 and LiteBIRD are designed to find them.
now.open_questions: Did inflation happen? If so, what drove it? The 'inflaton' field has no Standard Model identification.

items.reflection: Guth conceived inflation while preparing a lecture, scribbling 'spectacular realisation' in his notebook. The notebook page (1979) is reproduced in many textbooks. Even cosmology has Eureka moments.

moments.title: ALH84001 announcement
moments.who: David McKay and team, NASA Johnson Space Center
moments.body: On 7 August 1996, NASA announces possible evidence of past microbial life in Martian meteorite ALH84001, found in Antarctica's Allan Hills in 1984. Evidence: PAHs, magnetite crystals, microscopic shapes interpretable as fossilised bacteria. President Clinton addresses the nation. Subsequent analysis attributes all signatures to non-biological processes.
moments.takeaway: The most prominent claim of evidence for extraterrestrial life in the 20th century was withdrawn under scientific scrutiny. The methodology of biosignature claims tightened sharply afterward.

now.title: Astrobiology today
now.body: NASA's planetary protection rules prevent forward-contamination of potential biospheres. Perseverance's cached Mars samples may eventually be returned. Atmospheric biosignatures on exoplanets (JWST observations of K2-18b, 2023 — DMS claim contested) extend the methodology. The Drake equation's fl term remains unconstrained at 0 or 1 detections.
now.open_questions: What level of evidence would be required to claim discovery of extraterrestrial life? The bar is now much higher than in 1996.

items.reflection: President Clinton's 1996 address concluded: 'We will continue to listen closely to what it has to say as we continue the search for answers and for knowledge that is as old as humanity itself.' The search continues.

moments.title: New Horizons flies past Pluto
moments.body: Launched in 2006, New Horizons reaches Pluto on 14 July 2015 — and finds a geologically active world: nitrogen ice glaciers, water-ice mountains, a heart-shaped plain (Tombaugh Regio). At Pluto's distance, sunlight is ~1/1000 of Earth's. New Horizons later flies past Arrokoth (1 January 2019), a binary contact object in the Kuiper Belt.
moments.takeaway: Pluto turned out to be one of the most surprising worlds in the solar system. Smaller worlds are not necessarily dead worlds.

moments.title: Pluto reclassified
moments.body: On 24 August 2006, the IAU defines 'planet' such that Pluto becomes a 'dwarf planet'. The decision is controversial. Discoverer Clyde Tombaugh's widow protests. New Horizons launches months earlier — to a planet that becomes a dwarf planet en route.
moments.takeaway: Categories in science are conventions. Pluto did not change; the definition did.

now.title: Outer solar system today
now.body: The Kuiper Belt contains ~100,000 objects >100 km diameter. Eris, Haumea, Makemake, Sedna are major dwarf planets. The Vera Rubin Observatory (2025-) will discover thousands more. A hypothetical 'Planet Nine' (~6 Earth masses, ~400-800 AU) may explain orbital clustering of distant objects.
now.open_questions: Does Planet Nine exist? Surveys are searching.

items.reflection: When New Horizons launched (2006), Pluto was a planet. When it arrived (2015), it was a dwarf planet. The mission's principal investigator Alan Stern remains a vocal critic of the 2006 reclassification.

moments.title: Cassini-Huygens at Saturn
moments.body: Cassini orbits Saturn from 2004 to 2017, completing 294 orbits. Huygens (ESA) lands on Titan in 2005 — the most distant landing in history. Cassini discovers active water plumes from Enceladus (2005); samples them in flybys. Titan has methane lakes and complex organic chemistry. Mission ends with a controlled plunge into Saturn (15 September 2017) to prevent contamination of Enceladus.
moments.takeaway: A single 20-year mission transformed our view of the Saturn system from 'rings + moons' to 'multiple ocean worlds with active geology'.

now.title: Ocean worlds today
now.body: Europa, Enceladus, Titan, Ganymede, Callisto and Triton all have or may have subsurface oceans. Europa Clipper (launched 2024, arrives 2030) and JUICE (launched 2023, arrives 2031) will characterise Jupiter's icy moons. A Dragonfly drone mission to Titan launches in 2028.
now.open_questions: Could Enceladus or Europa host life in their oceans? Plume sampling is the most accessible path to answer.

items.reflection: Cassini was a joint NASA-ESA-ASI mission whose science return was so high it received funding extensions twice. International cooperation on flagship science missions remains the model — and is increasingly fragile politically.

moments.title: Bradley discovers stellar aberration
moments.body: Bradley, attempting to measure stellar parallax, instead discovers a different effect — stellar aberration, the small apparent shift in stars due to Earth's orbital motion combined with the finite speed of light. The effect is ~20.5 arcseconds in amplitude. Bradley uses it to refine Roemer's (1676) measurement of the speed of light to within 1%.
moments.takeaway: An attempt to measure one effect serendipitously discovered another — and confirmed Earth's motion around the Sun more directly than any earlier observation.

now.title: Aberration today
now.body: Stellar aberration is now a routine correction in astrometry. Gaia's microarcsecond astrometry must account for it precisely. Bradley's value of the constant of aberration is essentially correct (20.49552 arcseconds).
now.open_questions: How does relativistic aberration manifest at near-light-speed observations of distant sources?

items.reflection: Bradley was a clergyman before becoming Astronomer Royal (1742-62). The mathematics of light-time and motion that he established underpins every space-based positional measurement made today.

moments.title: Hale 200-inch goes online
moments.body: The Hale 200-inch (5.1m) telescope at Palomar is dedicated on 3 June 1948 after 20 years of construction (delayed by WWII). It remains the world's largest telescope until 1976. The mirror's 14.5-tonne Pyrex blank, cast at Corning Glass Works in 1934, took 11 months to cool and 11 years to grind and polish.
moments.takeaway: A single mirror dominated optical astronomy for 28 years. Big telescopes are decadal projects in design and decadal opportunities in science.

now.title: Big telescopes today
now.body: Keck I and II (10m each, 1993/1996, Mauna Kea), VLT (4x8.2m, ESO Chile, 1998-2001), Subaru (8.2m, 1999), GTC (10.4m, 2009). Under construction: Extremely Large Telescope (39m, ESO, first light expected 2028), Thirty Meter Telescope (paused over Mauna Kea siting), Giant Magellan Telescope (24.5m). The Vera Rubin Observatory (8.4m, 2025) will produce wide-field surveys.
now.open_questions: Are ground-based telescopes facing a satellite-constellation crisis? Starlink and other megaconstellations are increasingly contaminating optical observations.

items.reflection: George Ellery Hale built four record-breaking telescopes successively (Yerkes 40-inch refractor 1897, Mt Wilson 60-inch 1908, 100-inch 1917, 200-inch posthumous 1948). One person can shape an instrument culture for 50 years.

moments.title: Karl Jansky finds cosmic radio
moments.body: Investigating noise affecting transatlantic radio telephony, Jansky identifies a signal that repeats every 23 hours 56 minutes — the sidereal day. The source is in Sagittarius — the centre of the Milky Way. Radio astronomy is born from telephone-company maintenance work.
moments.takeaway: An entire new branch of astronomy began as a debugging investigation by an electrical engineer.

moments.title: 21cm hydrogen line detected
moments.who: Harold Ewen and Edward Purcell, Harvard
moments.body: Predicted by Hendrik van de Hulst (1944), the 21cm radio emission from neutral hydrogen is detected by Ewen and Purcell. This becomes the most-used line in radio astronomy — used to map galactic structure, measure cosmological redshifts, and search for SETI signals.
moments.takeaway: Hydrogen's quantum spin-flip transition radiates at 1420 MHz — universally — making it the radio astronomer's universal beacon.

now.title: Radio astronomy today
now.body: Arecibo (1963-2020), Very Large Array (1980, New Mexico), Lovell (Jodrell Bank), MeerKAT (South Africa), ALMA (Chile, mm wavelengths), FAST (China, 500m, 2016). The Square Kilometre Array (SKA, under construction in South Africa and Australia) will be the largest radio array. The EHT used VLBI radio interferometry to image black holes.
now.open_questions: What do the unexplained Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) come from? Magnetars are a leading candidate; some sources repeat in patterns.

items.reflection: Jansky's 1932 announcement was page-one news in the New York Times. Bell Labs decided not to fund follow-up; Jansky was reassigned. Grote Reber, an amateur, built a 9m radio dish in his Illinois backyard (1937) and continued the work. Radio astronomy began as amateur science.

moments.title: Spitzer Space Telescope
moments.body: Spitzer, launched 25 August 2003, observes in the mid-infrared from an Earth-trailing solar orbit. It surveys the galactic plane, discovers Saturn's huge outer Phoebe ring (2009), characterises the first exoplanet atmospheres (HD 209458b, HD 189733b), and discovers the TRAPPIST-1 system's seven planets. Mission ends January 2020.
moments.takeaway: A space telescope can quietly transform multiple subfields over 17 years without the public profile of Hubble.

now.title: Space telescopes today
now.body: JWST (infrared, 2021-), Hubble (optical/UV/near-IR, 1990- still operating), Gaia (astrometry, 2013-), TESS (transit photometry, 2018-), Euclid (cosmology, 2023-). Roman Space Telescope (planned 2027) will survey wide fields. China's CSST, India's Aditya-L1 and others extend international capability.
now.open_questions: Can Hubble be safely deorbited or extended? Commercial servicing missions are being studied.

items.reflection: Lyman Spitzer Jr proposed orbital telescopes in 1946 — 44 years before Hubble launched. Long-arc visions in astronomy require generations of follow-up.

moments.title: Falcon 9 first orbital booster landing
moments.body: On 21 December 2015, SpaceX successfully lands the first stage of a Falcon 9 rocket at Cape Canaveral after delivering 11 Orbcomm satellites. It's the first time an orbital-class booster has been recovered. Reuse becomes routine within years; by 2024 individual boosters have flown 20+ times.
moments.takeaway: A capability much of the rocket industry deemed economically irrelevant became the default model within a decade.

now.title: Spaceflight today
now.body: SpaceX dominates launch (90%+ of US orbital launches, ~75% of global mass to orbit in 2023). Starship (largest rocket ever built, 2024 test flights ongoing) targets Mars and lunar Starship-HLS lander. Blue Origin's New Glenn, Rocket Lab's Neutron, China's CASC and Long March 9, India's HLVM3 extend the field. Starlink (5,500+ active satellites) is reshaping internet and the night sky.
now.open_questions: How will space debris be managed at megaconstellation scale? Kessler syndrome risk is increasing.

items.reflection: Government space programs (NASA Apollo budget peaked at 4.4% of US federal spending; modern SpaceX revenue is a tiny fraction of that) now deliver more orbital mass per dollar by orders of magnitude. The economics of spaceflight shifted decisively in the 2010s.

moments.title: Baade and Zwicky predict neutron stars
moments.who: Walter Baade and Fritz Zwicky, Mt Wilson
moments.body: Zwicky and Baade propose that supernovae mark the collapse of ordinary stars into neutron stars made of nuclear matter — and that supernovae are the source of cosmic rays. The hypothesis predates the discovery of neutron stars (Bell, 1967) by 33 years.
moments.takeaway: Theoretical predictions of stellar end-states preceded their observational discovery by decades.

now.title: Stellar deaths today
now.body: Type Ia (white dwarf thermonuclear), Type II (core-collapse) and other supernova classifications now have detailed models. Neutron-star mergers (GW170817) are now known to produce heavy elements (kilonovae). The 1987A supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud was the closest naked-eye supernova since Kepler's (1604).
now.open_questions: What is the maximum mass of a neutron star? Recent measurements (PSR J0952-0607 at 2.35 M☉) push the limit; the equation of state of nuclear matter is the key uncertainty.

items.reflection: Zwicky was famously combative — he called other astronomers 'spherical bastards' (bastards from any angle). His predictions of neutron stars, supernovae as sources of cosmic rays, gravitational lensing and dark matter were each decades ahead of their time. Few astronomers have had so many ideas vindicated.

moments.title: WMAP and Planck precision
moments.body: WMAP (2001-10) maps CMB anisotropies with 13× the resolution of COBE; Planck (2009-13) with 3× the resolution of WMAP. Together they pin down the universe's age (13.787 ± 0.020 Gyr), composition (5% baryonic, 27% dark matter, 68% dark energy) and geometry (flat to within 0.4%).
moments.takeaway: Cosmology became a precision science: parameter uncertainties dropped from ~10% to ~1% within 20 years.

now.title: Precision cosmology today
now.body: DESI (Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, 2021-) is measuring BAO at 5x the precision of Planck. The Hubble tension (early-universe H₀ vs late-universe H₀) has resisted resolution and may indicate new physics. Future CMB experiments (LiteBIRD, CMB-S4, Simons Observatory) target B-mode polarisation.
now.open_questions: Is the Hubble tension new physics or systematics? DESI's 2024 results raised similar tension in dark energy equation-of-state.

items.reflection: Each precision improvement reveals more puzzles. Cosmology's precision era has not delivered a closed theory — it has narrowed remaining mysteries.

moments.title: GW170817 multi-messenger event
moments.body: On 17 August 2017, LIGO and Virgo detect a gravitational wave from two neutron stars merging in galaxy NGC 4993. Within seconds, the Fermi gamma-ray space telescope sees a short gamma-ray burst. Within hours, optical telescopes worldwide see the kilonova fade. Spectroscopy identifies heavy elements — gold, platinum, uranium — being created.
moments.takeaway: A single event observed across gravitational waves, gamma rays, X-rays, optical, infrared and radio confirmed that neutron star mergers produce heavy elements. The gold in jewellery comes from such mergers.

now.title: Multi-messenger astronomy today
now.body: IceCube (neutrinos), LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA (gravitational waves), Fermi (gamma rays), Vera Rubin Observatory (optical) coordinate alerts. Few multi-messenger events have occurred since GW170817 but the infrastructure is now built. LISA (2035) will detect supermassive black hole mergers.
now.open_questions: How frequent are detectable multi-messenger events? GW170817 was rare; the next nearby neutron star merger may be decades away.

items.reflection: GW170817 was such a coincidence (Fermi detected the gamma-ray burst 1.7 seconds after the GW) that it provided the strongest constraint on the speed of gravity matching the speed of light: |v_GW - c|/c < 10⁻¹⁵.

moments.title: Copernicus dies as his book is printed
moments.body: Copernicus, dying of a stroke, reportedly receives the first printed copy of 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium' on his deathbed (24 May 1543). The book had been suppressed and edited; a preface added by Andreas Osiander (without Copernicus's consent) presented heliocentrism as a calculating device rather than physical reality.
moments.takeaway: The book that began modern astronomy was completed only as its author died, and immediately framed as fiction to avoid theological controversy.

moments.title: Galileo's trial
moments.body: Galileo is tried for heresy after publishing 'Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems' (1632), defending Copernicus. He is forced to recant under threat of torture (22 June 1633) and lives under house arrest until his death in 1642. The Catholic Church formally rehabilitated Galileo only in 1992.
moments.takeaway: The institutional cost of advocating heliocentrism was real and lasting. Galileo's house arrest preceded scientific freedom by centuries.

now.title: Science and religion today
now.body: Catholic Church now formally accepts heliocentrism (and evolution). Conflicts persist over evolution teaching, climate science (less so) and bioethics (more so). Vatican Observatory (founded 1891) is a fully professional astronomical institution.
now.open_questions: Where do contemporary science-religion conflicts emerge? Cosmology's multiverse hypothesis and AI consciousness debates are likely frontiers.

items.reflection: It took 359 years for the Catholic Church to formally rehabilitate Galileo. Pope John Paul II acknowledged the 'tragic mutual incomprehension' in 1992. Institutional admissions of error can take longer than civilisations.

moments.title: Mayan astronomical precision
moments.body: Mayan astronomers track Venus's 584-day synodic period to an accuracy of within 1 day per 500 years, predict eclipses, and develop the Long Count calendar. The Dresden Codex (c.1100 CE, derived from earlier sources) contains tables of Venus and eclipse predictions used for ritual planning. Mayan zero was used independently in their numeral system (though India's mathematical zero was earlier).
moments.takeaway: Pre-contact American astronomers achieved precision matching contemporary Old World work, with no apparent exchange of techniques.

now.title: Indigenous astronomy today
now.body: Mauna Kea (Hawai'i) telescope controversies highlight tensions between modern astronomy and indigenous sacred-site protection. The Thirty Meter Telescope project has been on hold since 2019. Australian Aboriginal star knowledge (e.g. the Emu in the Sky) is being formally recognised in academic astronomy.
now.open_questions: Can modern astronomy infrastructure respect indigenous land claims? It is increasingly a precondition for siting decisions.

items.reflection: Of the four known Pre-Columbian Mayan codices, three are in European libraries (Dresden, Madrid, Paris) — taken during Spanish colonisation. The Maya have been recovering their own astronomical history from foreign archives.

moments.title: Transits of Venus and global expeditions
moments.body: International expeditions to time the rare transits of Venus (last pair: 2004, 2012; next: 2117) aim to measure the astronomical unit. Captain James Cook's first Pacific voyage (1769) takes him to Tahiti to observe the transit. Guillaume Le Gentil spends 11 years away from France, missing both transits to clouds and military upheavals.
moments.takeaway: International scientific cooperation organised the first global observation campaign 100 years before the Suez Canal. Astronomy invented the multi-national field campaign.

now.title: AU today
now.body: The astronomical unit is now defined as exactly 149,597,870,700 metres (2012 IAU resolution). Radar and spacecraft ranging measure solar system distances to centimetre precision. Cook's other voyages reshaped Pacific geography and indigenous Pacific populations were severely affected by introduced disease.
now.open_questions: What modern equivalent of the Venus transit drives global astronomy expeditions today? Eclipse expeditions remain communal, but the science is now done by spacecraft.

items.reflection: Le Gentil returned to France to find himself legally declared dead, his estate divided among heirs. Science can be patient; bureaucracy is not. Some heroes of science were also its martyrs to bad luck.
